title: Rare Orange ‘Pumpkin Spice’ Baby Loggerhead Turtle Spotted in Florida
summary:
Fall decorations showed up early in stores this year—and so did an unusually colorful baby sea turtle. In August, Florida resident Michael Landress saw a loggerhead hatchling (Caretta caretta) hurrying toward the ocean. Its shell had an earthy autumn tint. "'Pumpkin Spice' sprang to mind as the little orange hatchling raced to its ocean home," Landress wrote to Popular Science, even though he says he does not like pumpkin spice drinks or pie.

Most loggerhead hatchlings have dark-to-light brown top shells, called the carapace, and flippers that are dark with paler edges. Their bottom shell, the plastron, is usually tan or faded yellow, said Daniel Evans, a biologist at the Sea Turtle Conservancy. Colors as bold as "pumpkin spice," or albino turtles, are rare.

Color matters for camouflage. Hatchlings hide in floating seaweed mats such as sargassum. Typical browns blend in; odd colors stand out more to predators, Evans explained. That is likely why adults rarely show such dramatic hatchling color differences. Adult loggerheads usually have reddish-brown carapaces and pale yellowish undersides.

Loggerheads are named for their large heads. They live in subtropical and temperate seas, and Florida hosts one of the world's largest nesting groups. Still, the IUCN lists them as Endangered, and the United States lists them as Threatened. A major danger is accidental catch in commercial fishing gear.

The pumpkin-spice hatchling offers a gentle seasonal wonder: nature's palette can surprise even people who spend lots of time on Florida beaches.
